title: Session Hijacking

objectives.text: Explain why a stolen or guessed session token lets an attacker act as the user without the password or MFA
Tell hijacking from spoofing, active from passive hijacking, and map cases to ATT&CK T1539, T1550.004, T1185 and T1563
Recognize session fixation, session prediction, cookie theft through XSS, sidejacking, man-in-the-browser and CRIME/BREACH from their symptoms
Read tool output that points to weak sessions: ZAP cookie alerts and Burp Sequencer effective entropy
Explain why TCP hijacking depends on sequence numbers, and how random ISNs (RFC 6528) and challenge ACKs (RFC 5961) defend against blind, RST and injection attacks
Spot ARP spoofing, ICMP redirect and UDP race attacks from arpwatch or Wireshark clues, and name the matching defense
Pick the right control for each attack: Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite cookies, a new ID at login, timeouts, server-side logout, HSTS, IPsec
Describe how to detect hijacking: session binding and logging, WAF and IDS rules, manual versus automatic methods

readingMap.why: Learn the definitions, the two levels and the hijacking-vs-spoofing contrast; the ATT&CK table helps with scenario questions.
Most questions describe a web session weakness and ask for its name or fix: fixation, prediction, XSS theft, sniffing.
Know why sequence numbers matter, what blind, RST and UDP hijacking mean, and how ARP spoofing shows up in logs.
Matching each attack to its control (cookie flags, ID renewal, timeouts, HSTS, IPsec) is the most tested skill here.

labs.name: OWASP WebGoat session management lessons
labs.skill: Running WebGoat locally and working through its session lessons to see why weak session IDs and cookies fail

labs.name: Audit cookie attributes with an OWASP ZAP passive scan
labs.skill: Running OWASP Juice Shop in your own lab, proxying it through ZAP and reading the HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite cookie alerts

labs.name: Watch ARP pairings on your own lab network
labs.skill: Running arpwatch and Wireshark on a lab network you own and reading new station, changed ethernet address and flip flop reports

labs.name: Check HSTS and cookie settings of a site you run
labs.skill: Scanning your own site with the HTTP Observatory and fixing its HSTS header and session cookie attributes

feynmanPrompts: Explain to a web developer why an attacker holding someone's session cookie does not need their password or MFA code, and which three cookie attributes limit the damage.
Explain session fixation to a friend: why keeping the same session ID across login is the bug, and why issuing a new ID at login fixes it.
Explain why taking over a TCP connection used to be about guessing sequence numbers, and why randomized ISNs and encryption (TLS, SSH, IPsec) make it fail today.
